papers.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
papers.authors: Steven Yu, Sheng-Yu Wang, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba et al.
papers.summary: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

papers.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
papers.authors: Nhan Tran, Hijung Valentina Shin, Abe Davis, Mackenzie Leake
papers.summary: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

papers.title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
papers.authors: Moshe Shenfeld, Eliad Tsfadia, Katrina Ligett
papers.summary: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce propose-filter-release (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

papers.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gardès, Amil Dravid, Patrick Pérez et al.
papers.summary: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

papers.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
papers.authors: Jiongfan Yang, Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Zhongang Cai et al.
papers.summary: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

papers.title: SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
papers.authors: Yunchu Zhang, Ray Song, Junhan Jiao, Liyiming Ke et al.
papers.summary: Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools, including articulated ones, and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot.

papers.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
papers.authors: Quentin Dhôte, Romaric Audigier
papers.summary: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.

papers.title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
papers.authors: Derong Jin, Xiyi Chen, Ming C. Lin, Ruohan Gao
papers.summary: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

papers.title: SymAnt: Grounding Long-Horizon Action Anticipation with Adaptable Symbolic Priors
papers.authors: Fnu Aryan, Yaqi Xie, Joseph Campbell, Woojun Kim et al.
papers.summary: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.

papers.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
papers.authors: Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Itai Gat, Haiming Bao et al.
papers.summary: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of 10⁻³, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.

papers.title: Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies
papers.authors: Jiahua Li, Zixu John, Tom Zhong, Fuping Wu et al.
papers.summary: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at https://fight-world-model.github.io.

papers.title: A Conveyor Belt Mechanism for Repositionable Magnetic Coupling Between Continuum Robots
papers.authors: Ella Walsh, Eric Diller, Jessica Burgner-Kahrs
papers.summary: This work proposes a novel conveyor belt mechanism enabling continuous, active repositioning of functional elements along the body of a tendon-driven continuum robot. Up to three conveyor belt mechanisms are integrated within a 9 mm diameter continuum robot. We demonstrate equivalent or reduced conveyor belt actuation forces compared to robot tendon actuation forces. As a case study, we mount permanent magnets along two conveyor belts, and demonstrate actively reconfigurable inter-robot coupling. Coupling point location and quantity can be adjusted during robot operation to actively tune the effective stiffness of the coupled multi-robot system. We show that effective stiffness follows a predictable inverse-cubic relationship with coupling location, and increases with the number of coupling points. These findings demonstrate that the conveyor belt mechanism enables active functional element repositioning for changing tasks requirements, with magnetic inter-robot coupling as one proof-of-concept.

papers.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
papers.authors: Yuze He, Yixiang Wei, Wang Zhao, Chuhao Chen et al.
papers.summary: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

papers.title: Multistatic ISAC with Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression for 5G and Beyond
papers.authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Sastry Kompella
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity enable joint wireless sensing and communication using shared infrastructure and spectrum resources. While multistatic ISAC can increase sensing coverage with spatially distributed receivers, dense and dynamic clutter can significantly degrade bistatic range and Doppler estimation, leading to errors in target localization and velocity estimation. This paper presents a multistatic ISAC framework with clutter suppression for high-fidelity estimation of target position and velocity. Distributed clutter is modeled with randomly located scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections to capture dense and dynamic clutter effects. A broad range of conventional signal processing baselines are evaluated for clutter suppression, showing limited robustness under strong clutter conditions. To address this limitation, deep learning-based clutter suppression methods are introduced to improve robustness against dense and dynamic clutter by employing residual and attention-enhanced deep neural network architectures that directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations. These methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.

papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
papers.authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
papers.summary: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as π0.5. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics

papers.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
papers.authors: Francesco d'Amore, Joel Rybicki, Nobutaka Shimizu, Takeharu Shiraga et al.
papers.summary: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous h-Majority, in which every node independently samples h nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that h-Majority achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size h 3 and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within O(1+1h²p,1,nh) rounds, where n is the number of nodes and p is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for h-Majority that holds for every h3 and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within O( n/h²p,1) rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part I: Fundamentals
papers.authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco, Alessio Caporali, Miguel Aranda, Gianluca Palli et al.
papers.summary: In robotics, shape control (or shape servoing) refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object to achieve a desired shape. It involves a feedback loop that exploits the relation between robot motion and changes in the measured shape. This relation, known as the interaction Jacobian or, in this context, the deformation Jacobian, depends on the object's mechanical properties, geometry, and boundary conditions (e.g., where the object is grasped). Because these factors are often difficult to model accurately, the deformation Jacobian can be estimated locally from observed shape changes produced by commanded robot motions, without requiring a fine-tuned mechanical model. This article is the first of a two-part tutorial on data-driven Jacobian-based shape control of deformable objects. It introduces the central elements of the approach: the formulation of the shape-control problem, shape representation, estimation and online update of the deformation Jacobian, and a standard control law from the literature. It then assembles these elements into a complete shape-servoing loop, derives a local stability condition for this loop, and illustrates why some target shapes cannot be reached. Part II covers more advanced topics. Throughout both parts, a simulated planar example in which two robot arms manipulate an elastic rod observed by a camera illustrates the concepts.

papers.title: Power Adjusting Games Under Block-Dependent Pool Payout Schemes
papers.authors: Mustafa Doger, Sennur Ulukus
papers.summary: Advanced power adjusting block withholding attacks such as PAW and T-PAW have been analyzed so far under a global-reset version of the proportional scheme (GRP), which is rarely used in practice. In this paper, we analyze T-PAW, which contains FAW and PAW as special cases, under the block-dependent payout schemes deployed in practice: Pay-Per-Last-N-Shares (PPLNS), round-based Proportional (PROP) and exponential-decay (EXP). We derive the revenue ratios analytically, by renewal arguments for PPLNS and through the stationary carry process of an open round for PROP and EXP. We further introduce Power Adjusting Hopping (PAH), where an adversary of any size adjusts its power allocation towards the pool according to the blockwork age of the round without withholding any block, and derive its revenue ratios under PROP and EXP. We show that GRP misestimates the T-PAW gain in a scheme-dependent direction: it overstates the gain under PROP up to an order of magnitude and understates it under EXP for the original slush decay rate. PROP is highly vulnerable to PAH, while EXP faces a trade-off: a slow decay invites PAH and a fast decay invites T-PAW. PPLNS is the least vulnerable scheme: it is immune to PAH and it mitigates, but does not eliminate, T-PAW. All analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations.

papers.title: The Privacy and Security Risks of Edge LLM Optimization
papers.authors: Mingchen Li, Ren-Yi Huang, Dumindu Samaraweera, Prashant Shekhar et al.
papers.summary: Edge deployment of Large Language Models requires optimization techniques that reduce memory, computation, and energy costs. However, preserving task performance does not necessarily preserve security. We argue that optimization is an information transformation that can alter representations, decision pathways, and trust boundaries, creating security drift and optimization-induced attack surfaces.

papers.title: PhysVLMM: Interaction-Conditioned Physical Belief Maps for Articulated Objects in Robot Scene Maps
papers.authors: Dibyendu Ghosh
papers.summary: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.

papers.title: RecHash: Segmented Hash-Entangled Chains for Stateful Sequential Authentication
papers.authors: Luis Adrián Lizama-Pérez
papers.summary: RecHash is a stateful sequential authentication construction based on paired hash-chain openings and an authenticated record history. It develops the decreasing position relation of the 2019 hash-entangled construction, whose exact integer normalization yields a two-coordinate constant-sum antichain. Direct proportional reuse is constrained by integer capacity and multiplicative contraction. The main construction instead assigns each record to a predetermined chain segment, with complementary positions encoding each digest block. All digests fit every scheduled slot, independently of preceding messages. For an ℓ-bit digest distributed over k equal-length chain pairs, balanced allocation gives L/(2ℓ/k+1) slots. A 256-bit digest, 32 pairs, and length 65535 provide 254 application records followed by a renewal certificate, with 2048 bytes of openings per record for 256-bit chain outputs. We give a complete segmented state transition, a worked trace, exact allocation and resource results, and a renewal-free security-composition theorem conditional on authenticated history and an adaptive one-step guarantee. The analysis relates the construction to constant-sum encodings and standardized hash-based signatures; a concrete post-quantum reduction and security across renewal remain open.

papers.title: Discovering Interpretable Acoustic Features in Autoregressive Voice-Cloning TTS Models
papers.authors: Anuj Diwan, David Harwath, Eunsol Choi
papers.summary: Voice-cloning TTS models synthesize an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts, but it remains unclear which acoustic properties they represent and use. We introduce a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, analyzing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions via sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability. We focus on Qwen3-TTS and extend probing and steering to 5 additional models to test generalization across architectures. These models encode concepts like pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering are effective only for some concepts. Strong probing does not always translate to steering or vice-versa. SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds 684 automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond known concepts. Overall, we perform a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models.

papers.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure – Past experiences and future strategies
papers.authors: Gergely Sipos, Sergio Andreozzi, Marco Rorro, Andrea Manzi et al.
papers.summary: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

papers.title: SPECTRUM: A Strategic Framework and Technical Blueprint for European Exascale Research Data and Compute Infrastructure
papers.authors: Sergio Andreozzi, Stefano Bagnasco, Florian Berberich, Tommaso Boccali et al.
papers.summary: The HiLumi LHC, the SKA Observatory and LOFAR 2.0 will take High Energy Physics (HEP) and Radio Astronomy (RA) towards exabyte-scale data within the next decade, beyond the capacity of today's infrastructure. The SPECTRUM project responded with two documents built on the same evidence. A Technical Blueprint describes a European compute and data continuum as a capability map, consolidates the gaps found in HEP, RA and related use cases, and recommends technical actions in eight areas. A Strategic Research, Innovation and Deployment Agenda (SRIDA) organises thirteen priorities in four pillars, maps them to investment areas and European funding instruments, and phases them over a roadmap set against the timelines of the three instruments. This paper, by editors and contributors of both documents, summarises them, their consultative method and the impact the SRIDA expects.

papers.title: Can We Rely on Language Models to Orchestrate Services across the Edge-Cloud Continuum?
papers.authors: Zhenghao Wu, Ruihai Dong, Reza Farahani, Hamed Haddadi et al.
papers.summary: Service orchestration across the edge–cloud continuum increasingly uses language models (LMs) to translate intents and operational evidence into scheduling, configuration, diagnosis, and remediation decisions. Yet, useful model outputs do not by themselves establish dependable orchestration: reliability also depends on where the LM enters the decision process, what authority it is granted, how actions are constrained, and what system-level evidence supports the claimed effect. Existing surveys provide limited synthesis of the links between continuum-specific orchestration decisions, LM responsibility, operational authority, assurance controls, and supporting empirical evidence. We systematically review 39 primary studies and develop a five-dimensional analytical framework for connecting system context, orchestration decisions, LM agency, operational safeguards, and evaluation evidence. The synthesis reveals predominantly hybrid designs in which LMs support interpretation, candidate generation, and mitigation planning, while downstream components commonly retain feasibility enforcement and execution authority. Bounded closed-loop remediation is emerging, but continuum-specific constraints remain unevenly represented in decision formulations, and production-scale evidence across heterogeneous edge–cloud environments remains limited. These findings suggest that reliance on LM-enabled orchestration depends on aligning decision constraints, operational authority, safeguards, and evaluation evidence with the claimed system effect.

papers.title: Bridging Neural Representations and Symbolic Semantics in Audio Classification
papers.authors: Avishek Das, Pascal Hitzler
papers.summary: Deep audio classifiers can achieve strong predictive performance, but their hidden representations remain difficult to interpret. Existing audio explainability methods often focus on input-level attribution, such as waveform segments, spectrogram regions, or acoustic features, and provide limited insight into what hidden neurons encode. Interpreting hidden neurons at the concept level can provide a more meaningful view of what an audio model learns internally. This paper investigates whether hidden neurons in audio classifiers can be associated with human-understandable symbolic acoustic concepts. A model-agnostic neurosymbolic framework is presented for analyzing the final hidden layer of audio classifiers, containing 32 neurons, through symbolic concept induction. The framework is evaluated on two audio classification settings: music genre classification using GTZAN dataset and musical instrument classification using IRMAS dataset. Results show that several hidden neurons can be associated with meaningful induced concepts, and most confirmed neuron-concept pairs are statistically supported using the Mann-Whitney U test. These findings suggest that symbolic concept induction is a promising direction for explaining latent audio representations beyond input-level attribution.

papers.title: Deep Learning Based Behavioral Drift Modeling for Continuous Biometric Authentication
papers.authors: Suprava Saha Dibya, Minar, Abdulla Al Noman, Md. Zafir Abid Shresto et al.
papers.summary: This research proposes a two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system that provides defense-in-depth security through continuous behavioral drift monitoring. Level 1 employs fixed-text password authentication using Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT), achieving 3.77% EER for high-security login verification. Upon successful authentication, Level 2 continuously monitors user typing during natural free-text sessions using a 4-Model Deep Learning Ensemble. If suspicious behavioral drift is detected during monitoring, the system re-authenticates the user by returning to Level 1, providing a feedback loop against session hijacking and behavioral anomalies. The system explicitly models long-term behavioral drift through the fixed-text component's PBT mechanism, which adapts to temporal variations in password typing patterns. This research leverages free-text (Buffalo dataset) and fixed-text (GREYC dataset) keystroke dynamics datasets, extracting temporal and spatial features including hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals, and trigram patterns. The final system achieves 96%+ accuracy for fixed-text authentication (3.77% EER) and 83.53% True Acceptance Rate (TAR) at 5% False Acceptance Rate (FAR) for free-text continuous authentication (10.05% EER), demonstrating superior performance and strong resistance to impostor attacks through continuous behavioral monitoring.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
papers.authors: Ezra Edelman, Benjamin Edelman, Surbhi Goel, Eran Malach
papers.summary: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.

papers.title: What Makes a Good Audio Prompt for Zero-Shot TTS? Learning Prompt Selection from Synthesis Outcomes
papers.authors: Arnon Turetzky, Yossi Adi
papers.summary: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) models clone a target voice from a short reference clip, commonly referred to as the prompt. In practice, the prompt has to be cut from a longer recording of the speaker, so which part to use must be chosen. To understand what makes a good prompt, we analyze hundreds of thousands of outputs synthesized by four TTS models from candidate prompts of YouTube recordings. The choice of prompt substantially changes intelligibility, naturalness and speaker similarity. Standard predicted-quality scores capture mainly the naturalness part but miss most of the intelligibility gain. We find that the models largely agree on which prompt yields the highest measured speaker similarity, but much less on which prompt yields intelligible speech. We propose a small network that learns from the outputs a TTS model produced to rank a recording's candidate prompts from their audio alone. Without synthesizing anything at selection time, it picks prompts that lower the word error rate on held-out recordings by a third (Qwen3-TTS) to two fifths (F5-TTS) relative to a randomly chosen prompt, more than predicted quality achieves and nearly as much as synthesizing a dozen test sentences from every candidate first.

papers.title: Manual binding and semi-automated interface generation for efficient simulation backends with user-friendly frontends: A demonstration for epidemic use cases
papers.authors: Maximilian Betz, Daniel-Michel Richter, Daniel Abele, René Schmieding et al.
papers.summary: Challenges and chances of mathematical software are directly entangled with the programming language used. Depending on the background of developers and users, conflicts between different goals may arise. While several, e.g., scripting languages allow a low barrier and user-friendly entry to mathematical modeling and simulation, corresponding implementations will most likely not allow timely outcomes for detailed simulations. In infectious disease modeling, while several large-scale software frameworks rely on C or C++ implementations, most models are implemented in Python or R. While the latter allow for fast prototyping and more interactive development, it has been shown for several applications that C or C++ implementations outperform plain Python or R implementations by factors between one and three orders of magnitude. In particular, in times of pandemics, the urgent need for swift estimation of the system's dynamics makes the use of large-scale models in these noncompiled languages prohibitive. In order to create synergies and close the gap between scientists from the application and the computational domain, binding libraries allow to execute entire, compiled software frameworks from languages such as Python. However, with iterative model development, extension, or addition of new models, implementing bindings can represent another relevant barrier to developers of the C or C++ backends. In this paper, we show how a large-scale software framework with a multitude of infectious disease models can be efficiently exposed to Python. In addition, we suggest a semi-automated way to generate interface code by analyzing generic C++ code through abstract syntax trees, enabling a modularized approach working with intermediate representations.

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
papers.summary: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.

papers.title: True 3D Holography: A Communication Service of Tomorrow and Its Requirements for a New Converged Cloud and Network Architecture on the Path to 6G
papers.authors: Ingo Friese, Mandy Galkow-Schneider, Louay Bassbouss, Alexander Zoubarev et al.
papers.summary: Research project 6G NeXt is considering true 3D holography as a use case, setting requirements on the communication as well as the computing infrastructure. In a future holographic communication service, clients are widely spread in the network and cooperatively interact with each other. Especially for holographic communication high processing power is required as well. This makes a high-speed distributed backbone computing infrastructure, which realizes the concept of split computing, inevitable. Furthermore, tight integration between processing facilities and wireless networks is required in order to provide an immersive user experience. This paper illustrates true 3D holographic communication and its requirements. Afterward, an appropriate solution approach is elaborated. Here, novel technological approaches are discussed based on a proposed overall communication and computing architecture.

papers.title: Towards fNIRS foundation models: A curated corpus of 67 public datasets with channel positions in MNI space
papers.authors: Santiago Posso-Murillo
papers.summary: Brain foundation models have transformed medical artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience by reducing the reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While they have been successful with non-invasive neuroimaging data, their adoption in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has lagged due to the limited size and heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and sensor configurations. In addition, no single fNIRS dataset is comparable in size to the largest datasets in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). The fNIRS datasets are also spread across different platforms and often have insufficient information, or lack the protocols that would make them easier to use. Given the advances in EEG foundation models that enable flexible modeling across diverse EEG montages, we curated 1,955 hours of fNIRS data from 67 public datasets spanning 2,798 participants, representing the largest fNIRS curation effort to date. The curated data include oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated (HbR) hemoglobin signals along with the three-dimensional position of every channel in the standard space of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI), which makes positions comparable across datasets. We release dataloaders that handle each dataset automatically, along with the minimal preprocessing pipeline used to prepare the data, at https://github.com/sposso/fnirs-datasets. This work aims to facilitate the future development of foundation models for fNIRS.

papers.title: When Modernization Breaks Working Code: A Single-File Study of LLMs on Legacy PHP
papers.authors: Afridi Mahmud, Abid Hasan Khondaker, Sadif Ahmed, Md Nafiu Rahman et al.
papers.summary: Pasting a legacy file into an LLM and asking it to "modernize this" is an easy shortcut. But is the result better than leaving the code alone? In this paper, we study this single-file setting with five LLMs, each asked to modernize 100 WordPress 4.0 PHP files to PHP 8.3 while preserving behavior, with no project context or execution feedback. We evaluate every output with 630 hidden behavioral checks and 511 Rector-detected modernization findings. We compare against two baselines: the unchanged originals and the rule-based tool Rector. Often, the answer is no. Untouched, 83 files already pass every check; the best LLM leaves only 59. Each model breaks 32-51 working files while repairing at most 10, whereas Rector breaks 7 and repairs 6. Most of this damage is unnecessary. Only 37 findings (7 percent) require a change under PHP 8.3, yet in compatible files with no required change, the LLMs break 36-60 percent (Rector: 8 percent). The model with the highest modernization score is no more compatible than its closest competitors. Most regressed checks come from files that no longer load at all, often because of type declarations PHP itself rejects. These are errors that need no project context to avoid. Evaluations of LLM-based modernization should therefore measure against a no-change baseline and report modernization and behavioral preservation separately.

papers.title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
papers.authors: Yishuo Cai, Minzheng Wang, Liang Zhao, Linghao Zhang et al.
papers.summary: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.

papers.title: Unraveling the Efficacy of Neuron Coverage Criteria on Testing Large Language Models
papers.authors: Xiaoning Ren, Jiayang Song, Chongyang Liu, Jie Li et al.
papers.summary: Neuron coverage criteria aim to assess test suite quality and guide test input generation, but their effectiveness for Transformer-based language models remains unclear. We evaluate six criteria, including four established and two recent criteria, across encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder models. Our evaluation examines error-revealing capability, distribution diversity, sample fairness (category diversity), and guidance for test input generation. The results reveal uneven effectiveness. Erroneous samples provide only 0.32% additional coverage over noise samples, indicating limited sensitivity to adversarial errors. By contrast, coverage criteria effectively assess distribution diversity and sample fairness in 26 and 30 of 33 configurations, respectively. Incorporating neuron-wise coverage guidance into test input generation increases adversarial sample production by only 4.56%. These findings suggest that existing coverage criteria can serve as an antidote for assessing diversity but remain largely a placebo for revealing adversarial errors, particularly when used individually. Their practical value therefore depends on whether these limited benefits justify the computational overhead of testing large Transformer-based models. Our study highlights the need for more robust and efficient coverage criteria tailored to these models, with stronger error-revealing capability and greater value for test generation.

papers.title: "It Feels Weird to Just Rely on AI": How Experienced Healthcare Professionals Work With Decision Support Systems in Clinical Practice
papers.authors: Simon W. S. Fischer, Hanna Schraffenberger, Miranda L. van Hooff, Casper Reijnen et al.
papers.summary: Decision support systems (DSS) assist with clinical decision-making. Little is known, however, about the decision-making process with DSS in clinical practice and the extent to which clinicians consider or rely on the predictions. Studies on human-AI decision-making usually focus on laypeople, simplified decision tasks, or one-shot interactions with prototypes that are not integrated into existing workflows. To gain insights from real-world practice, we conducted an online survey (n=12) and semi-structured interviews (n=10) with clinicians from two different medical cohorts each working with a DSS. Findings show, amongst other things, that the interaction with DSS changes as experience increases, the predictions become more important in complex cases, that decisions are discussed with colleagues, and that workflow integration affects decision-making. Our findings on human, technical, contextual, and organisational factors contribute to a socio-technical perspective on DSS reliance behaviour. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the design of DSS.

papers.title: Apple Vision Pro: The good, the bad, the ugly
papers.authors: Santiago Berrezueta-Guzman, Andrei Koshelev, Habiba-Loai Khalil, Stefan Wagner
papers.summary: Apple Vision Pro (AVP), the headset Apple introduced as its first ``spatial computer,'' built by a single, vertically integrated vendor, entered the market in February 2024 and has since accumulated a fast-growing body of primary research spanning surgery, education, accessibility, design, and human-computer interaction. In this paper, we adopt the tripartite structure of Leone's 1966 film to organize a systematic review of this literature: we cataloged the validated, working applications of AVP (the good), the persistent technical and ergonomic limitations of a still-early-generation headset (the bad), and the ethical concerns and structural harms that follow from deliberate design, marketing, and deployment choices (the ugly). The review is built from a Scopus export of 218 records mentioning AVP, which we narrowed to 104 papers (2024–2026) with a primary focus on AVP, using explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria that we report in full, alongside a PRISMA-informed flow diagram of the screening process. We find the corpus heavily skewed toward validating benefits (medicine and surgery, education, and software tooling account for over half of the included papers) and comparatively thin on documented risks or misuse, a pattern we treat as a finding in its own right rather than a limitation to be explained away. We further show that several recurring issues, namely price, simulated social presence, and the gaze-tracking privacy architecture, resist a clean separation into ``bad'' or ``ugly'' using the published evidence alone, since both readings remain compatible with the same data. We close by identifying where the evidence base most needs to grow: independent risk and ethics research, bystander- and equity-focused study designs, and disclosure that would let researchers distinguish an engineering backlog from a structural choice.

papers.title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
papers.authors: Peter Dolog, Kim G. Larsen, Marius Mikučionis, Frederik F. K. Rasmussen
papers.summary: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.

papers.title: Greenscapes: Optimized Vegetation Configurations in Cities
papers.authors: Patryk Bartkowiak, Marcin Marlewski, Paweł Wójcik, Jae Joong Lee et al.
papers.summary: Vegetation plays a central role in cities, serving functional roles such as balancing shade and sky exposure, shaping the microclimate, carbon sequestration, and providing acoustic screening. Furthermore, aesthetic choices in landscape styles (formal, modernist, picturesque) are important for citizens' well-being and should be considered in the design of urban landscapes. In this paper, we present a novel method for placing vegetation, ranging from shrubs to large trees, in 3D urban scenes. Our method uses individual lots as input and employs a conditioned Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate a top-down rendering of vegetation, placing large trees, small trees, and shrubs on lawn areas. This rendering is then converted into a 3D scene by detecting individual plants and selecting appropriate 3D assets. To refine the proposed configurations, we define an optimization loop that keeps the VLM-generated positions fixed after a deterministic feasibility repair and uses CMA-ES to optimize per-instance scale transformations along with discrete vegetation asset substitutions. To define the objective function for the optimization, we evaluate the generated 3D scenes with efficient surrogate models of shade and path-based acoustic exposure. Furthermore, we render in-scene views at each optimization step to compute view-dependent perceptual descriptors, enabling the generation of both aesthetic and functional vegetation layouts for urban scenes.

papers.title: Mastering Multi-State Dynamics: Continuum Damage and Viscoplastic MPM for RL-Based Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Yusen Feng, Shangbo Luan
papers.summary: Robotic manipulation of multi-state materials needs a simulator that handles large deformation, topology change, and two-way contact between tools and materials while staying fast enough to drive online reinforcement learning. We present MG-CD-MPM, a tool-centered localized extension of CD-MPM. The implicit Ginzburg-Landau phase-field damage system is solved on a local patch by preconditioned conjugate gradients using a geometric-multigrid V-cycle as the preconditioner. The background MPM discretization remains uniform: only the damage solve is localized. Two-way rigid-tool coupling converts MPM contact impulses into forces and torques on the tool, exposing material resistance directly to the policy. The resulting Gym-like simulator covers soft solids, brittle materials, granular media, and viscoplastic or semi-fluid media within a unified per-particle constitutive layer. We demonstrate cutting, scooping, and shoveling in six scenes, combining scripted tool motions with PPO policies trained on two cutting tasks.

papers.title: Inkitiate: Initiating and Steering Agent Assistance through Ink in a Spatial Workspace
papers.authors: Liangwei Wang, Nan Chen, Luna K. Qiu, Zilong Wang et al.
papers.summary: Handwriting and sketching help people develop ideas around information. As this work unfolds, users may seek assistance with finding, understanding, and organizing materials. We investigate how ink can initiate and steer agent assistance in this process. An eight-participant formative study explored desired assistance and interaction expectations, informing three connected activities: bringing materials in, thinking with materials, and shaping the space. We present Inkitiate, a spatial workspace for ink-based agent assistance in knowledge work. Through ink, users retrieve external materials, build on accumulated content and results, and reorganize the canvas, while inspecting and guiding agent actions. In a study with eighteen participants, users reported favorable usability and low perceived workload, and used retained ink and materials to develop further ink queries. An ink-query vocabulary and cases reveal how users combine linguistic and graphical expressions to direct agents. These findings inform ink-based agent interaction design for expressive requests and continued work with materials.

papers.title: ExploreRepair: Evidence-Specialized Agents for Vulnerability Repair under Information Constraints
papers.authors: Duc Manh Tran, Ratnadira Widyasari, Ivana Clairine Irsan, Huihui Huang et al.
papers.summary: Automated vulnerability repair must often operate with incomplete vulnerability information: developers may lack an accurate vulnerability classification or a provided proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) test, yet still need to produce a repair. Without detailed information, a key challenge is to explore multiple plausible interpretations of the vulnerability before committing to a repair. To address this challenge, we propose ExploreRepair, a vulnerability repair framework that reconciles the vulnerability observations and repair implementations from a team of exploration agents. We first collect these observations and repair implementations from three agents, each tasked with exploring a specific dimension of the vulnerability. Then, a Lesson Aggregator and a Patch Aggregator independently synthesize repairs from these observations and concrete implementations before a final Aggregator reconciles their proposals without benchmark feedback. On PatchEval, ExploreRepair achieves repair success rates of 39.6% and 71.6% with GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, exceeding EvoRepair, a state-of-the-art vulnerability repair approach, by 16.0 and 25.4 percentage points. On VulnLoc+, it achieves success rates of 51.4% and 62.9%, respectively, exceeding LoopRepair's variant without PoV tests by 20.0 and 17.1 percentage points.

papers.title: Ambisonics: Introducing an Accessible, Distributed Approach
papers.authors: Thomas A Rushton, Romain Michon, Tanguy Risset, Clemens Wegener et al.
papers.summary: This paper presents an accessible, distributed approach to higher order ambisonics using a network of low-cost microcontroller-based devices. Leveraging recent advances in embedded computing, networked audio, and precise time synchronization, the system offers an alternative to conventional centralized architectures that typically require expensive multichannel interfaces and high-performance digital signal processing hardware. The proposed architecture combines an audio plugin for soundfield design with a modular network of ambisonics processing units, which, exploiting the parallelisable nature of ambisonics decoding, are each responsible for a subset of loudspeaker outputs. Synchronization is achieved through the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol, complemented by adaptive clock correction to maintain sub-microsecond alignment between devices. A third-order ambisonics implementation demonstrates the viability of the approach, with potential scalability to higher orders and larger arrays. Overall, this work contributes to the development of frugal, distributed solutions for immersive audio, expanding access to ambisonics-based systems for a wide range of applications.

papers.title: AKDQ: Adaptive Key-Delta Quantization for Low-Bitrate RVQ-based Neural Speech Codecs
papers.authors: Xiao-Hang Jiang, Yang Ai, Zhen-Hua Ling, Ji Wu
papers.summary: Low-bitrate speech coding is essential for bandwidth-constrained channels and on-device applications, but conventional residual vector quantization (RVQ)-based codecs employ a fixed number of codebooks per frame regardless of content. Adjacent speech frames often exhibit strong similarity, and quantizing them independently with the same scheme results in redundant encoding, thereby wasting bitrate. Therefore, we propose Adaptive Key-Delta Quantization (AKDQ), which replaces the fixed per-frame VQ allocation of RVQ with an adaptive frame-wise key-or-delta policy. AKDQ is a plug-in strategy that requires no modification to the codec's encoder-decoder backbone. Specifically, in AKDQ, each frame is classified as either a key-frame (K-frame) quantized with all VQs, or a delta-frame (D-frame) quantized with only a few VQs on a delta correction from the previous reconstruction, thereby reducing bitrate. The K/D decision is made by a budget-aware causal scheduler through a bit-bank mechanism, keeping the system streamable with no additional lookahead. Experiments on both causal and non-causal codec families demonstrate that AKDQ effectively reduces bitrate redundancy. For instance, on DAC, using AKDQ at 1.5 kbps achieves reconstruction quality comparable to using the baseline RVQ at 2.0 kbps, saving 25% of the bitrate.

papers.title: SpeakerTurn: Target-Speaker Semantic Turn Detection in Multi-Speaker Environments
papers.authors: Nan Li, Hetao Shan, Jintao Liang, Jiahao Yan et al.
papers.summary: Semantic completeness alone cannot determine when an assistant should respond in a multi-speaker environment: a completed utterance may belong to an interfering speaker, while the designated user is still speaking, acknowledging, or requesting time. We therefore study semantic turn inference conditioned on speaker identity. We propose SpeakerTurn, a framework that jointly predicts the target transcript and turn state from a speech mixture and an independent target-speaker reference. Built on CocktailASR-1, it links semantic decisions to the corresponding target content through joint supervision, distinguishing complete, incomplete, backchannel, wait, and target-absent states, with a separate interruption task. We also examine whether structured chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision improves decisions by representing speaker presence and semantic cues. On a synthetic multi-speaker test set, SpeakerTurn achieves five-state macro F1 of 0.811 and target-transcription character error rate (CER) of 4.20%, correctly resolving all ten reference-swapped interruption pairs. Joint-format transcription and native-interface recognition nevertheless behave differently, and CoT improves validation transcription without improving turn macro F1. These results show why target attribution, semantic turn discrimination, and recognition retention require separate assessment when adapting speech language models for speaker-conditioned interaction.

papers.title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
papers.authors: Chen Su, Xingqun Qi, Xurui Hu, Bingkun Yang et al.
papers.summary: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities (i.e., object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor, a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG), which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical (e.g., root to body to hand to objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation.

papers.title: Trajeform: Embedding Crowd Data
papers.authors: Marilena Lemonari, Panayiotis Charalambous, Yiorgos Chrysanthou
papers.summary: Crowd simulation aims to generate agent behaviours that are rich, natural, and appropriate to their surrounding environment. Recent advances in Machine Learning have enabled such behavioural patterns to be learned directly from trajectory data, allowing simulation models to capture increasingly complex crowd dynamics. However, the capabilities of these systems remain strongly dependent on the type and diversity of the data used during training. When evaluating how well crowd simulators generalise to real-world datasets, most existing metrics focus primarily on trajectory-level differences rather than behaviour-level similarity. In this paper, we present Trajeform, a framework that trains a reconstruction VAE (Variational Autoencoder) on real trajectory data to learn a meaningful continuous embedding that preserves behavioural characteristics of real crowds. The trained encoder can then be applied to synthetic trajectories generated by simulators and used to compare the resulting embedding distributions. Additionally, the learned embedding can be used to analyse supplementary data, such as trajectories corresponding to a simulator's principal behaviours or captured data from controlled environments (e.g., cycling), providing insight into their ability to span the real behavioural embedding space. The framework compares data from three simulators (CCP, modCCP, and RVO) against ground-truth datasets and is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively using latent-space analysis, distributional metrics, and trajectory generation through sampling from the aggregated posterior distribution. The results indicate that the learned latent space captures meaningful trajectory dependencies found in the real data, making the framework useful both as an additional measure of synthetic data believability and as a tool for informing the training of future trajectory models.

papers.title: DeepDiff: Neuro-Dynamic Regression-Freedom Checking for Security Patch Validation
papers.authors: Laboni Sarker, Shuvendu K Lahiri
papers.summary: Automatically validating AI-generated security patches remains a significant challenge. Eliminating a reported crash and passing existing test suites do not provide sufficient confidence that a patch correctly addresses the underlying vulnerability without introducing regressions. We present DeepDiff, a technique for regression-freedom checking that differentially evaluates candidate patches against the original vulnerable program using non-crashing inputs that exercise the affected code paths. The expectation of regression-freedom is that a correct patch should eliminate the vulnerability triggering crash while preserving the intended behavior on non-crashing inputs. To support this evaluation, we introduce a dataset of correct and incorrect patch candidates for open-source memory-safety vulnerabilities from CyberGym. We explore different approaches for non-triggering test input generation to reach the patched code, a purely neural regression-freedom checker, and a hybrid approach that combines dynamic analysis with neural techniques. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of regression-freedom checking in validating security patches while outlining the challenges that remain.

papers.title: HEARSAYBENCH: Can AI Navigate from Abstract Human Rights to Lived Lives?
papers.authors: Ava Iranmanesh, Sobhan Lotfi, Ali Iranmanesh, Liwei Jiang
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse. We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. HEARSAYBENCH makes this failure measurable, a step toward systems that serve the world as it is rather than as assumed.

papers.title: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs
papers.authors: Zhipin Wang, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Christoph Leiter, Steffen Eger
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by 5.6%–17.9%, while most increase diversity by 10.2%–18.1% when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In 79.3% of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas (r=0.70). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

papers.title: When Does Closed-Loop Curriculum Adaptation Help GRPO? An Analysis on Countdown
papers.authors: Yuv Raj Pant, Moshiur Rahman Tonmoy, Kaiqun Fu
papers.summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model's current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN, a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer.
